```{r}
lego <- read.csv("case-study2-data.csv")
```

## Exploratory Data Analysis: Theme, Pieces, Minifigures, and Unique Pieces (Gavin)

### 1. Data Preparation

#### 1.1 Variable Types and Missing Values

```{r}
View(lego)
```

```{r}
## EDA — Theme, Pieces, Minifigures, and Unique Pieces
### Data Preparation
# Convert Amazon_Price from text (e.g., "$19.99") to a number
lego$Amazon_Price <- as.numeric(gsub("[$,]", "", lego$Amazon_Price))
# Check the structure of the variables we will analyze
str(lego[, c("Amazon_Price", "Theme", "Pieces",
             "Minifigures", "Unique_Pieces")])
# Count missing values in our variables
colSums(is.na(lego[, c("Amazon_Price", "Theme", "Pieces",
                       "Minifigures", "Unique_Pieces")]))
```

#### 1.2 Cleaning LEGO Theme Names

```{r}
# Save the original theme names in case we need them later
lego$Theme_Original <- lego$Theme
# Convert theme names to plain ASCII text
# This removes problematic special characters
lego$Theme <- iconv(
  lego$Theme,
  from = "",
  to = "ASCII",
  sub = ""
)
# Remove any extra spaces
lego$Theme <- trimws(lego$Theme)
# Check the most common themes after cleaning
head(sort(table(lego$Theme), decreasing = TRUE), 15)
```

### 2. Theme Analysis

#### 2.1 Number of LEGO Sets by Theme

```{r}
# Count how many LEGO sets belong to each theme
theme_counts <- sort(table(lego$Theme), decreasing = TRUE)

# Display the 15 most common themes
head(theme_counts, 15)
```

#### 2.2 LEGO Theme Prevalence — Word Cloud

```{r}
library(wordcloud)

# Count LEGO sets by theme
theme_counts <- sort(table(lego$Theme), decreasing = TRUE)

# Create clean theme names for the word cloud
theme_names <- iconv(
  names(theme_counts),
  from = "latin1",
  to = "ASCII",
  sub = ""
)

# Create the word cloud
set.seed(470)

wordcloud(
  words = theme_names,
  freq = as.numeric(theme_counts),
  min.freq = 2,
  max.words = 30,
  random.order = FALSE,
  rot.per = 0,
  scale = c(3.5, 0.7),
  colors = c(
    "#1F77B4",  # Blue
    "#FF7F0E",  # Orange
    "#2CA02C",  # Green
    "#D62728",  # Red
    "#9467BD",  # Purple
    "#17BECF",  # Teal
    "#E377C2",  # Pink
    "#BCBD22",  # Olive
    "#8C564B",  # Brown
    "#E6A23C",  # Gold
    "#264653",  # Dark teal
    "#E76F51"   # Coral
  ),
  ordered.colors = FALSE
)
```

#### 2.3 Median Amazon Price by LEGO Theme

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Calculate median Amazon price and number of priced sets by theme
theme_prices <- lego |>
  filter(!is.na(Theme), !is.na(Amazon_Price)) |>
  group_by(Theme) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    median_price = median(Amazon_Price),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(n >= 10)

# Plot median Amazon price for themes with at least 10 priced sets
ggplot(theme_prices,
       aes(x = reorder(Theme, median_price), y = median_price)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2878B5") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Amazon Price by LEGO Theme",
    subtitle = "Themes with at least 10 sets with available Amazon prices",
    x = "LEGO Theme",
    y = "Median Amazon Price"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

#### 2.4 LEGO Theme and Amazon Price Distribution — Heat Map

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Keep sets with known themes and Amazon prices
theme_heatmap <- lego |>
  filter(!is.na(Theme), !is.na(Amazon_Price)) |>

  # Group Amazon prices into ranges
  mutate(
    Price_Range = cut(
      Amazon_Price,
      breaks = c(0, 25, 50, 100, 200, Inf),
      labels = c("$0–25", "$25–50", "$50–100",
                 "$100–200", "$200+"),
      include.lowest = TRUE
    )
  ) |>

  # Count sets in each theme and price range
  count(Theme, Price_Range, name = "Count") |>

  # Keep themes with at least 10 sets with known prices
  group_by(Theme) |>
  filter(sum(Count) >= 10) |>
  ungroup()

# Create heat map
ggplot(
  theme_heatmap,
  aes(
    x = Price_Range,
    y = reorder(Theme, Count, FUN = sum),
    fill = Count
  )
) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "#EAF3F8",
    high = "#145A86"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "LEGO Theme Distribution Across Amazon Price Ranges",
    subtitle = "Number of sets in each theme and price category",
    x = "Amazon Price Range",
    y = "LEGO Theme",
    fill = "Number of Sets"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)
  )
```

### 2.5 Percentage Distribution of Amazon Prices Within Each LEGO Theme

```{r}
# Calculate the percentage of sets in each price range within each theme
theme_heatmap_pct <- theme_heatmap |>
  group_by(Theme) |>
  mutate(
    Percentage = 100 * Count / sum(Count)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

# Create percentage-based heat map
ggplot(
  theme_heatmap_pct,
  aes(
    x = Price_Range,
    y = reorder(Theme, Percentage, FUN = max),
    fill = Percentage
  )
) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "#EAF3F8",
    high = "#145A86",
    limits = c(0, 100),
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Amazon Price Distribution Within Each LEGO Theme",
    subtitle = "Percentage of priced sets in each price range",
    x = "Amazon Price Range",
    y = "LEGO Theme",
    fill = "Percentage"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1)
  )
```

### 3. Pieces Analysis

#### 3.1 Distribution of LEGO Piece Counts

```{r}
# Summary statistics for the number of pieces
summary(lego$Pieces)

# Histogram showing the distribution of piece counts
ggplot(lego, aes(x = Pieces)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 40,
    fill = "#2878B5",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_comma()
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of LEGO Set Piece Counts",
    subtitle = "Number of pieces per LEGO set",
    x = "Number of Pieces",
    y = "Number of LEGO Sets"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

#### 3.2 Relationship Between Pieces and Amazon Price

```{r}
# Keep sets with known piece counts and Amazon prices
pieces_price <- lego |>
  filter(!is.na(Pieces), !is.na(Amazon_Price))

# Calculate the Pearson correlation
cor(pieces_price$Pieces, pieces_price$Amazon_Price)

# Scatterplot of piece count and Amazon price
ggplot(pieces_price, aes(x = Pieces, y = Amazon_Price)) +
  geom_point(
    color = "#2878B5",
    alpha = 0.5,
    size = 2
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE,
    color = "#E76F51",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(
    title = "Relationship Between LEGO Pieces and Amazon Price",
    subtitle = "Scatterplot with fitted linear trend",
    x = "Number of Pieces",
    y = "Amazon Price"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

#### 3.3 Log-Log Relationship Between Pieces and Amazon Price

```{r}
# Keep observations with positive piece counts and Amazon prices
pieces_price_log <- pieces_price |>
  filter(Pieces > 0, Amazon_Price > 0)

# Create a scatterplot with logarithmic axes
ggplot(
  pieces_price_log,
  aes(x = Pieces, y = Amazon_Price)
) +
  geom_point(
    color = "#2878B5",
    alpha = 0.5,
    size = 2
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE,
    color = "#E76F51",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(
    labels = scales::label_comma()
  ) +
  scale_y_log10(
    labels = scales::label_dollar()
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "LEGO Pieces vs. Amazon Price (Log-Log Scale)",
    subtitle = "Logarithmic axes highlight patterns across set sizes",
    x = "Number of Pieces (Log Scale)",
    y = "Amazon Price (Log Scale)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

### 6. Additional Data Quality Investigation

#### 6.1 Missing Minifigure Counts by LEGO Theme

```{r}
# Calculate missing minifigure counts by theme
minifig_missing <- lego |>
  filter(!is.na(Theme)) |>
  group_by(Theme) |>
  summarise(
    Total_Sets = n(),
    Missing_Minifigures = sum(is.na(Minifigures)),
    Missing_Percent = 100 * mean(is.na(Minifigures)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(Total_Sets >= 10) |>
  arrange(desc(Missing_Percent))

# Display missingness by theme
print(minifig_missing, n = Inf)

# Visualize missingness
ggplot(
  minifig_missing,
  aes(x = reorder(Theme, Missing_Percent), y = Missing_Percent)
) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2878B5") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Missing Minifigure Data by LEGO Theme",
    subtitle = "Themes with at least 10 sets",
    x = "LEGO Theme",
    y = "Percentage Missing"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

### 7. Summary of Exploratory Findings

#### Theme

-   LEGO themes differ considerably in their typical Amazon prices. Creator Expert has the highest median price among the themes analyzed, while DOTS and Classic are among the lowest.

-   The word cloud shows that Star Wars, Friends, City, and NINJAGO are the most prevalent themes in the dataset.

-   The percentage-based heat map reveals that Amazon price distributions vary across themes, suggesting that Theme may be useful for predicting price.

#### Pieces

-   Total piece counts are strongly right-skewed, with a median of 198 pieces and a maximum of 6,020.

-   Pieces has a strong positive correlation with Amazon Price (r = 0.8117).

-   The log-log scatterplot shows an approximately linear positive relationship, suggesting that logarithmic transformations may be worth exploring during modeling.

#### Minifigures

-   Recorded minifigure counts are right-skewed, with a median of 2 and a maximum of 28.

-   Minifigures has a moderate positive correlation with Amazon Price (r = 0.5618).

-   Missing minifigure data is strongly associated with Theme. Several themes have 100% missing values, indicating that missingness may reflect differences in set characteristics or data collection.

#### Unique Pieces

-   Unique piece counts are right-skewed, with a median of 83 and a maximum of 1,067.

-   Unique_Pieces has a strong positive correlation with Amazon Price (r = 0.7061).

-   Pieces and Unique_Pieces are also strongly correlated (r = 0.7794), suggesting that they may contain overlapping predictive information.

#### Overall Conclusions

-   All three numerical variables examined have positive associations with Amazon Price, with Pieces showing the strongest pairwise linear correlation.

-   Theme also appears to be associated with price, although differences may partly reflect variation in set sizes.

-   Missing data, especially for Amazon_Price and Minifigures, will require careful consideration during predictive modeling.

-   Future modeling should evaluate whether Theme, Minifigures, and Unique_Pieces improve price predictions beyond what can be achieved using total piece count alone.

# Exploratory Data Analysis: Year, Ages, Price, and Amazon

### 1. Data preparation and quality checks

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)

# The supplied CSV uses Latin-1 text, including the one-half symbol in Ages.
# Read a fresh copy so this section can also run independently of earlier EDA.
lego_eda <- readr::read_csv(
  "case-study2-data.csv",
  locale = readr::locale(encoding = "Latin1"),
  na = c("", "NA", "N/A"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

required_columns <- c("Item_Number", "Set_Name", "Theme", "Year", "Ages",
                      "Price", "Amazon_Price", "Pieces", "Pages",
                      "Minifigures", "Unique_Pieces", "Availability")
stopifnot(all(required_columns %in% names(lego_eda)))

# Convert dollar strings to numbers, retaining original strings for auditing.
money_to_numeric <- function(x) {
  as.numeric(gsub("[$,[:space:]]", "", as.character(x)))
}

lego_eda <- lego_eda |>
  mutate(
    Price_Original = Price,
    Amazon_Price_Original = Amazon_Price,
    Price = money_to_numeric(Price),
    Amazon_Price = money_to_numeric(Amazon_Price),
    Year = as.integer(Year),
    Year_Group = factor(Year, levels = sort(unique(Year))),
    Amazon_Observed = !is.na(Amazon_Price),
    Amazon_Status = factor(
      if_else(Amazon_Observed, "Observed", "Missing"),
      levels = c("Observed", "Missing")
    )
  )

# Normalize Ages_6 - 12 to 6-12 and convert 1 1/2 (the half symbol) to 1.5.
# Ages_NA is a missing age recommendation, not an actual age category.
lego_eda$Ages_Clean <- trimws(sub("^Ages_", "", lego_eda$Ages))
lego_eda$Ages_Clean <- gsub("[[:space:]]", "", lego_eda$Ages_Clean)
lego_eda$Ages_Clean <- gsub("\u00bd", ".5", lego_eda$Ages_Clean, fixed = TRUE)
lego_eda$Ages_Clean[lego_eda$Ages_Clean %in% c("", "NA", "N/A")] <- NA_character_

# A '+' label has a lower age recommendation but no stated upper bound.
# Do not replace the absent upper bound with an arbitrary age.
age_pattern <- "^[0-9]+(\\.[0-9]+)?(\\+|-[0-9]+(\\.[0-9]+)?)$"
age_parse_issues <- lego_eda |>
  filter(!is.na(Ages_Clean), !grepl(age_pattern, Ages_Clean)) |>
  distinct(Ages, Ages_Clean)
print(age_parse_issues)
if (nrow(age_parse_issues) > 0) {
  stop("Unrecognized Ages labels: inspect age_parse_issues before continuing.")
}

lego_eda <- lego_eda |>
  mutate(
    Age_Min = as.numeric(sub("[+-].*$", "", Ages_Clean)),
    Age_Max = as.numeric(if_else(
      grepl("-", Ages_Clean), sub("^.*-", "", Ages_Clean), NA_character_
    )),
    Age_Format = case_when(
      is.na(Ages_Clean) ~ "Missing recommendation",
      grepl("+", Ages_Clean, fixed = TRUE) ~ "Minimum age (+)",
      TRUE ~ "Age range"
    )
  )

# Order full age labels by their lower bound, then their upper bound.
age_levels <- lego_eda |>
  filter(!is.na(Ages_Clean)) |>
  distinct(Ages_Clean, Age_Min, Age_Max) |>
  arrange(Age_Min, Age_Max, Ages_Clean) |>
  pull(Ages_Clean)
lego_eda$Age_Label <- factor(lego_eda$Ages_Clean, levels = age_levels)
lego_eda$Age_Min_Group <- factor(
  lego_eda$Age_Min, levels = sort(unique(na.omit(lego_eda$Age_Min)))
)

# Missingness across the ORIGINAL variables, with Ages_NA treated as missing.
missing_values <- vapply(lego_eda[seq_len(15)], function(x) sum(is.na(x)), integer(1))
missing_values["Ages"] <- sum(is.na(lego_eda$Ages_Clean))
missing_summary <- tibble(
  Variable = names(missing_values),
  Missing = unname(missing_values),
  Percent_Missing = 100 * Missing / nrow(lego_eda)
) |>
  arrange(desc(Percent_Missing))
print(missing_summary, n = Inf)

# Report potential problems without silently deleting sets or outliers.
quality_checks <- tibble(
  Check = c("Duplicate full rows", "Duplicate item numbers",
            "LEGO prices that did not parse", "Amazon prices that did not parse",
            "Nonpositive LEGO prices", "Nonpositive Amazon prices",
            "Years outside 2018-2020", "Age ranges with upper < lower",
            "Unique pieces greater than total pieces"),
  Count = c(
    sum(duplicated(lego_eda[seq_len(15)])),
    sum(duplicated(lego_eda$Item_Number)),
    sum(!is.na(lego_eda$Price_Original) & is.na(lego_eda$Price)),
    sum(!is.na(lego_eda$Amazon_Price_Original) & is.na(lego_eda$Amazon_Price)),
    sum(lego_eda$Price <= 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(lego_eda$Amazon_Price <= 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(!is.na(lego_eda$Year) & !lego_eda$Year %in% 2018:2020),
    sum(lego_eda$Age_Max < lego_eda$Age_Min, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(lego_eda$Unique_Pieces > lego_eda$Pieces, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
)
print(quality_checks, n = Inf)

# A reusable summary that handles groups with no observed values.
numeric_summary <- function(x) {
  observed <- x[is.finite(x)]
  q <- if (length(observed) > 0) {
    quantile(observed, c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1), names = FALSE)
  } else {
    rep(NA_real_, 5)
  }
  tibble(
    N_Observed = length(observed), N_Missing = sum(is.na(x)),
    Mean = if (length(observed) > 0) mean(observed) else NA_real_,
    SD = if (length(observed) > 1) sd(observed) else NA_real_,
    Minimum = q[1], Q1 = q[2], Median = q[3], Q3 = q[4], Maximum = q[5]
  )
}

eda_orange <- "#E76F51"
```

### Interpretation notes

-   Year is a release-year category. The 2020 sample ends on September 11, so raw counts do not measure a full year of production.
-   Ages are set recommendations, not ages of purchasers. Minimum-age plots combine ranges and '+' labels; the full-label plots preserve that distinction.
-   Amazon price summaries use observed prices. Missingness comparisons help assess whether the priced subset differs from other sets.
-   Positive discounts mean Amazon is cheaper than LEGO's recommended price. The comparison uses only sets with both prices observed.
-   Price outliers are flagged for review and remain in the analysis. Raw and log scales show different aspects of the distribution.
-   Pairwise correlations use different numbers of observations. Their sample sizes are reported alongside the correlation tables.
-   Minifigures recorded as NA can mean either no minifigures or missing data; they are not automatically changed to zero.
-   These are exploratory associations. Formal modeling and a fitted-model generalizability check remain separate steps.

# Additional Modeling for Amazon Price

These sections run independently of the earlier EDA. They read a fresh copy of
`case-study2-data.csv` from the project folder and leave the EDA objects unchanged.
Run the chunks in order. Install the packages listed in the first chunk if needed.
Results and figures are written to the relative `modeling-results` folder.

The presentation compares regressions and LASSO, but their fitting code and exact
split are not in the supplied QMD. This workflow establishes a new reproducible
comparison. It does not reproduce the slides' reported RMSE or provide independent
confirmation using a new dataset. Sets in this split may have appeared in the
earlier analyses.

We select a model by **RMSE in dollars** from repeated cross-validation in the
development sample. MAE shows performance when large errors receive less extra
weight. We keep the calibration and test samples out of model selection. The
LEGO recommended price, item numbers, set names, and anything derived from price
are excluded from all predictors. Amazon price is used only as the response.

## 1. Setup and an independent modeling dataset

The response must be observed and positive to train or evaluate a price model.
We retain all such sets even when predictors are missing. Age labels become their
minimum recommendations, and weight is expressed in kilograms. We retain unknown
minifigure counts as missing because an NA can represent either zero or unavailable
information. No expensive set is removed simply because its price is unusual.

```{r amz-model-1}
amz_packages <- c("readr", "dplyr", "ggplot2", "randomForest")
amz_missing_packages <- amz_packages[!vapply(amz_packages, requireNamespace,
                                          logical(1), quietly = TRUE)]
if (length(amz_missing_packages)) {
  stop("Install the missing packages first: install.packages(c(",
       paste(sprintf('"%s"', amz_missing_packages), collapse = ", "), "))")
}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
amz_show_plot <- function(p) {
  if(interactive() || isTRUE(getOption("knitr.in.progress"))) print(p)
}
amz_data_file <- "case-study2-data.csv"
amz_output_dir <- "modeling-results"
dir.create(amz_output_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
if (!file.exists(amz_data_file)) {
  stop("Place case-study2-data.csv beside this script/QMD and run from that folder.")
}
amz_seed <- 4702026
amz_folds <- 5L
amz_repeats <- 2L
amz_interval_level <- 0.90
amz_raw <- readr::read_csv(amz_data_file,
  locale = readr::locale(encoding = "Latin1"),
  na = c("", "NA", "N/A"), show_col_types = FALSE)

amz_number <- function(x) {
  suppressWarnings(readr::parse_number(as.character(x), na = c("", "NA", "N/A")))
}
amz_clean <- function(raw) {
  required <- c("Item_Number", "Set_Name", "Amazon_Price", "Theme", "Pieces",
    "Unique_Pieces", "Minifigures", "Year", "Ages", "Pages", "Weight",
    "Size", "Packaging", "Availability")
  stopifnot(all(required %in% names(raw)))
  age <- trimws(sub("^Ages_", "", as.character(raw$Ages)))
  age <- gsub("[[:space:]]", "", age)
  age <- gsub("\u00bd", ".5", age, fixed = TRUE)
  age[is.na(age) | age %in% c("", "NA", "N/A")] <- NA_character_
  valid_age <- is.na(age) | grepl("^[0-9]+(\\.[0-9]+)?(\\+|-[0-9]+(\\.[0-9]+)?)$", age)
  if (!all(valid_age)) stop("Unrecognized Ages labels: ", paste(unique(age[!valid_age]), collapse=", "))
  weight_text <- as.character(raw$Weight)
  weight <- amz_number(weight_text)
  pounds_only <- !is.na(weight_text) & grepl("lb", weight_text, ignore.case=TRUE) &
    !grepl("kg", weight_text, ignore.case=TRUE)
  weight[pounds_only] <- weight[pounds_only] / 2.2046226218
  out <- data.frame(
    Item_Number = as.character(raw$Item_Number), Set_Name = as.character(raw$Set_Name),
    Amazon_Price = amz_number(raw$Amazon_Price),
    Pieces = amz_number(raw$Pieces), Unique_Pieces = amz_number(raw$Unique_Pieces),
    Minifigures = amz_number(raw$Minifigures), Pages = amz_number(raw$Pages),
    Weight = weight, Age_Min = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(sub("[+-].*$", "", age))),
    Theme = as.character(raw$Theme), Year = as.character(raw$Year),
    Size = as.character(raw$Size), Packaging = as.character(raw$Packaging),
    Availability = as.character(raw$Availability), stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
  for (v in c("Theme", "Year", "Size", "Packaging", "Availability")) {
    out[[v]] <- trimws(out[[v]])
    out[[v]][out[[v]] %in% c("", "NA", "N/A")] <- NA_character_
  }
  for (v in c("Pieces", "Unique_Pieces", "Minifigures", "Pages", "Weight", "Age_Min")) {
    out[[v]][!is.finite(out[[v]]) | out[[v]] < 0] <- NA_real_
  }
  out
}
amz_all <- amz_clean(amz_raw)
if (anyDuplicated(amz_all$Item_Number)) stop("Duplicate set IDs need review before splitting.")
if (any(amz_all$Amazon_Price <= 0, na.rm=TRUE)) stop("Review nonpositive Amazon prices before modeling.")
amz_observed <- amz_all[is.finite(amz_all$Amazon_Price) & amz_all$Amazon_Price > 0, ]
amz_unpriced <- amz_all[!is.finite(amz_all$Amazon_Price), ]
print(data.frame(All_Sets=nrow(amz_all), Observed_Amazon=nrow(amz_observed),
                 Missing_Amazon=nrow(amz_unpriced)))
amz_predictor_missingness <- data.frame(
  Predictor=c("Pieces","Unique_Pieces","Minifigures","Pages","Weight","Age_Min",
              "Theme","Year","Size","Packaging","Availability"))
amz_predictor_missingness$Missing_Among_Priced <- vapply(
  amz_observed[amz_predictor_missingness$Predictor],function(x) sum(is.na(x)),integer(1))
print(amz_predictor_missingness)
# Price, names, and IDs never enter a design matrix. Price is read separately
# only after model selection for the LEGO-price generalizability check.
```

## 2. Development, calibration, and test samples

The 826 priced sets are split into an 80% training pool (660 sets) and a final
test sample (166). The training pool is further divided into 528 development sets
and 132 calibration sets. Development data support repeated 5-fold CV. Calibration
data determine prediction interval width after the model is selected. The test
data provide the final error and interval coverage estimates. Stratification by
release year and price group helps distribute the observations across samples.

```{r amz-model-2}
if (!exists("amz_output_dir")) amz_output_dir <- "modeling-results"
dir.create(amz_output_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

# This NEW split is not a reproduction of the presentation's unavailable split.
# Its rows may overlap sets used earlier, so it is not an independent new dataset.
# The 80% training pool contains a development sample and an interval-calibration
# sample. Calibration outcomes do not choose the model or fit its coefficients.
amz_strata <- function(dat) {
  rank_bin <- pmin(5L, ceiling(5 * rank(dat$Amazon_Price, ties.method="first") / nrow(dat)))
  interaction(dat$Year, rank_bin, drop=TRUE)
}
amz_sample_fraction <- function(dat, fraction, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  groups <- split(seq_len(nrow(dat)), amz_strata(dat))
  take <- unlist(lapply(groups, function(i) i[sample.int(length(i), floor(length(i)*fraction))]))
  wanted <- floor(nrow(dat)*fraction)
  if (length(take)<wanted) {
    remaining <- setdiff(seq_len(nrow(dat)),take)
    take <- c(take,remaining[sample.int(length(remaining),wanted-length(take))])
  }
  sort(take)
}
amz_pool_i <- amz_sample_fraction(amz_observed, 0.80, amz_seed)
amz_pool <- amz_observed[amz_pool_i, ]
amz_test <- amz_observed[-amz_pool_i, ]
amz_dev_i <- amz_sample_fraction(amz_pool, 0.80, amz_seed+1L)
amz_development <- amz_pool[amz_dev_i, ]
amz_calibration <- amz_pool[-amz_dev_i, ]
amz_split_table <- data.frame(
  Sample=c("Development and cross-validation", "Interval calibration", "Final test"),
  Sets=c(nrow(amz_development), nrow(amz_calibration), nrow(amz_test)))
print(amz_split_table)
amz_membership <- bind_rows(
  mutate(amz_development[c("Item_Number", "Set_Name")], Sample="Development"),
  mutate(amz_calibration[c("Item_Number", "Set_Name")], Sample="Calibration"),
  mutate(amz_test[c("Item_Number", "Set_Name")], Sample="Test"))
write.csv(amz_membership, file.path(amz_output_dir,"sample-membership.csv"), row.names=FALSE)
```

## 3. Preprocessing learned only from the current training sample

Every CV fit learns its own medians, rare-category groups, spline knots, and
design columns using only that fold's training rows. This avoids borrowing
information from the assessment fold. Missing numeric values receive training
medians plus missingness indicators. Categories with fewer than 10 training sets
are grouped, except release year and brick size. Unseen levels map to Other, and
the final prediction export flags unseen categories for review.

```{r amz-model-3}
if (!exists("amz_output_dir")) amz_output_dir <- "modeling-results"
dir.create(amz_output_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

amz_num <- c("Pieces", "Unique_Pieces", "Minifigures", "Pages", "Weight", "Age_Min")
amz_cat <- c("Theme", "Year", "Size", "Packaging", "Availability")
amz_learn_prep <- function(train) {
  medians <- vapply(train[amz_num], function(x) {
    if (all(is.na(x))) return(0)
    median(x, na.rm=TRUE)
  }, numeric(1))
  maps <- lapply(amz_cat, function(v) {
    x <- train[[v]]; x[is.na(x)] <- "Missing"
    counts <- sort(table(x), decreasing=TRUE)
    keep <- if(v %in% c("Year", "Size")) names(counts) else names(counts)[counts>=10]
    keep <- union(keep, intersect("Missing", names(counts)))
    mapped <- ifelse(x %in% keep, x, "Other")
    ref <- names(sort(table(mapped), decreasing=TRUE))[1]
    list(keep=keep, levels=c(ref, sort(setdiff(union(mapped,"Other"),ref))), seen=unique(x))
  }); names(maps) <- amz_cat
  filled_pieces <- train$Pieces; filled_pieces[is.na(filled_pieces)] <- medians["Pieces"]
  list(medians=medians, categories=maps,
       piece_spline=splines::ns(log1p(filled_pieces), df=3),
       ranges=lapply(train[amz_num], function(x) range(x,na.rm=TRUE)))
}
amz_design <- function(dat, prep, style) {
  # Observed zeros remain zeros. Unknown Minifigures get a training median and
  # a separate missingness indicator, rather than being assumed to mean zero.
  nums <- dat[amz_num]
  miss <- as.data.frame(lapply(nums, function(x) as.numeric(is.na(x))))
  names(miss) <- paste0(amz_num,"_Missing")
  for(v in amz_num) nums[[v]][is.na(nums[[v]])] <- prep$medians[v]
  if(style=="pieces") { vars <- "Pieces"; cats <- character() }
  else if(style %in% c("eda","eda_age_year")) {
    vars <- c("Pieces","Unique_Pieces","Minifigures"); cats <- "Theme"
    if(style=="eda_age_year") {vars <- c(vars,"Age_Min"); cats <- c(cats,"Year")}
  } else if(style=="spline") {
    vars <- c("Pieces","Minifigures","Age_Min"); cats <- c("Theme","Year","Size")
  } else { vars <- amz_num; cats <- amz_cat }
  x <- nums[vars]
  if(style %in% c("spline","transformed")) {
    for(v in setdiff(vars,"Age_Min")) x[[v]] <- log1p(x[[v]])
  }
  if(style=="spline") {
    x$Pieces <- NULL
    basis <- predict(prep$piece_spline, log1p(nums$Pieces))
    for(j in seq_len(ncol(basis))) x[[paste0("Pieces_Spline",j)]] <- basis[,j]
  }
  x <- cbind(x, miss[paste0(vars,"_Missing")])
  for(v in cats) {
    mp <- prep$categories[[v]]
    values <- dat[[v]]; values[is.na(values)] <- "Missing"
    values[!values %in% mp$keep] <- "Other"
    # Drop the reference dummy. Unused columns are handled at fit time.
    for(lev in mp$levels[-1]) x[[paste(v,lev,sep="__")]] <- as.numeric(values==lev)
  }
  names(x) <- make.names(names(x), unique=TRUE)
  stopifnot(!anyNA(x), !any(grepl("Amazon|Price|Set_Name|Item_Number",names(x))))
  x
}
```

## 4. Candidate models and prediction functions

The candidates include a mean-price benchmark, a piece-count regression, an
EDA-variable regression, an expanded regression, and an EDA model adding year and
age. Log-price regression uses a natural spline for log piece count and a smearing
correction when returning to dollars. A Gamma model uses a log link to model a
positive conditional mean directly. Ridge penalties address overlapping predictors.
Random forests provide a comparison allowing nonlinear relationships and interactions.
The log forest uses out-of-bag residuals for its smearing correction. All models
receive the same nonnegative prediction constraint before scoring.

```{r amz-model-4}
if (!exists("amz_output_dir")) amz_output_dir <- "modeling-results"
dir.create(amz_output_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

# Different lambda/mtry values are candidates selected by development CV.
# Ridge uses standardized predictors and the objective MSE + lambda*sum(beta^2).
amz_specs <- data.frame(
  Model=c("Training mean", "Pieces linear", "EDA linear", "Expanded linear",
          "Log price spline", "Gamma log spline", "Ridge 0.01", "Ridge 0.1",
          "Ridge 1", "Forest dollars mtry 4", "Forest dollars mtry 8", "Forest log price"),
  Engine=c("mean",rep("lm",4),"gamma",rep("ridge",3),rep("forest",3)),
  Style=c("pieces","pieces","eda","expanded","spline","spline",
          rep("transformed",6)),
  Log_Response=c(FALSE,FALSE,FALSE,FALSE,TRUE,FALSE,FALSE,FALSE,FALSE,FALSE,FALSE,TRUE),
  Lambda=c(rep(NA_real_,6),0.01,0.1,1,rep(NA_real_,3)),
  Mtry=c(rep(NA_integer_,9),4L,8L,4L), stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
amz_specs <- rbind(amz_specs,data.frame(Model="EDA plus year and age",Engine="lm",
  Style="eda_age_year",Log_Response=FALSE,Lambda=NA_real_,Mtry=NA_integer_))
amz_fit <- function(train, spec, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  prep <- amz_learn_prep(train)
  xx <- amz_design(train, prep, spec$Style)
  y <- train$Amazon_Price
  yy <- if(spec$Log_Response) log(y) else y
  nonconstant <- vapply(xx,function(x) length(unique(x))>1L,logical(1))
  x <- xx[,nonconstant,drop=FALSE]
  result <- list(spec=spec, prep=prep, columns=names(x), smear=1)
  if(spec$Engine=="mean") {
    result$fit <- mean(y)
  } else if(spec$Engine %in% c("lm","gamma")) {
    # Keep a full-rank training design, with exactly the same columns at predict time.
    qr_x <- qr(cbind(Intercept=1,as.matrix(x)))
    kept <- sort(qr_x$pivot[seq_len(qr_x$rank)])
    cols <- setdiff(colnames(qr_x$qr)[kept],"Intercept")
    result$columns <- cols
    frame <- data.frame(response=yy,x[,cols,drop=FALSE],check.names=FALSE)
    result$fit <- if(spec$Engine=="lm") {
      lm(response ~ ., data=frame, x=TRUE,y=TRUE)
    } else {
      glm(response ~ ., data=frame, family=Gamma(link="log"),
          control=glm.control(maxit=100),x=TRUE,y=TRUE)
    }
    if(spec$Engine=="gamma" && !result$fit$converged) stop("Gamma model did not converge")
    if(spec$Log_Response) result$smear <- mean(exp(residuals(result$fit)))
  } else if(spec$Engine=="ridge") {
    mat <- as.matrix(x)
    result$center <- colMeans(mat); result$scale <- apply(mat,2,sd)
    zz <- scale(mat,center=result$center,scale=result$scale)
    result$intercept <- mean(yy)
    result$fit <- solve(crossprod(zz)+nrow(zz)*spec$Lambda*diag(ncol(zz)),
                        crossprod(zz,yy-result$intercept))
  } else if(spec$Engine=="forest") {
    result$fit <- randomForest::randomForest(x=x,y=yy,ntree=400,
      mtry=min(spec$Mtry,ncol(x)),nodesize=5,importance=TRUE)
    # OOB residuals avoid using optimistic in-sample forest residuals to estimate smearing.
    if(spec$Log_Response) result$smear <- mean(exp(yy-result$fit$predicted),na.rm=TRUE)
  }
  result
}
amz_predict <- function(object, newdata) {
  x <- amz_design(newdata,object$prep,object$spec$Style)[,object$columns,drop=FALSE]
  engine <- object$spec$Engine
  pred <- if(engine=="mean") rep(object$fit,nrow(newdata)) else if(engine=="ridge") {
    zz <- scale(as.matrix(x),center=object$center,scale=object$scale)
    as.numeric(object$intercept+zz%*%object$fit)
  } else if(engine=="gamma") as.numeric(predict(object$fit,newdata=x,type="response"))
  else as.numeric(predict(object$fit,newdata=x))
  if(object$spec$Log_Response) pred <- exp(pred)*object$smear
  if(any(!is.finite(pred))) stop("Nonfinite predictions: inspect model extrapolation.")
  pmax(0,pred) # Prices cannot be negative; apply the same constraint before scoring.
}
amz_metrics <- function(actual,predicted) {
  stopifnot(length(actual)==length(predicted),all(is.finite(actual)),all(is.finite(predicted)))
  data.frame(N=length(actual),RMSE=sqrt(mean((predicted-actual)^2)),
    MAE=mean(abs(predicted-actual)),Bias=mean(predicted-actual),
    R2=if(sum((actual-mean(actual))^2)>0) 1-sum((predicted-actual)^2)/sum((actual-mean(actual))^2) else NA_real_)
}
```

## 5. Repeated cross-validation and model selection

We use the same assessment folds for all candidates, including the ridge and
forest tuning settings. All medians and category decisions are refitted within
each fold. A model must finish every assessment fold to be eligible. The model
with the lowest pooled CV RMSE is selected before any calibration or test errors
are examined. CV estimates used for choosing among candidates can be optimistic;
the reserved test sample assesses the selected procedure. Small differences in
CV error should not be treated as proof of a meaningful advantage.

```{r amz-model-5}
if (!exists("amz_output_dir")) amz_output_dir <- "modeling-results"
dir.create(amz_output_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

amz_cv_predictions <- list(); amz_cv_failures <- list(); amz_counter <- 0L
for(rep_i in seq_len(amz_repeats)) {
  set.seed(amz_seed+100L+rep_i)
  fold_id <- integer(nrow(amz_development))
  for(i in split(seq_len(nrow(amz_development)),amz_strata(amz_development))) {
    fold_id[i] <- sample(rep(seq_len(amz_folds),length.out=length(i)))
  }
  for(fold_i in seq_len(amz_folds)) {
    assessment <- which(fold_id==fold_i)
    fold_train <- amz_development[-assessment,]
    fold_assess <- amz_development[assessment,]
    for(j in seq_len(nrow(amz_specs))) {
      spec <- amz_specs[j,,drop=FALSE]
      value <- tryCatch({
        fit <- amz_fit(fold_train,spec,amz_seed+1000L*rep_i+100L*fold_i+j)
        data.frame(Model=spec$Model,Repeat=rep_i,Fold=fold_i,
          Item_Number=fold_assess$Item_Number,Actual=fold_assess$Amazon_Price,
          Predicted=amz_predict(fit,fold_assess))
      },error=function(e) e)
      amz_counter <- amz_counter+1L
      if(inherits(value,"error")) {
        amz_cv_failures[[length(amz_cv_failures)+1L]] <- data.frame(
          Model=spec$Model,Repeat=rep_i,Fold=fold_i,Reason=conditionMessage(value))
      } else amz_cv_predictions[[length(amz_cv_predictions)+1L]] <- value
    }
  }
  message("Completed cross-validation repeat ",rep_i," of ",amz_repeats)
}
amz_cv_predictions <- bind_rows(amz_cv_predictions)
amz_cv_failures <- bind_rows(amz_cv_failures)
amz_cv_summary <- amz_cv_predictions |>
  group_by(Model) |>
  summarise(Predictions=n(),CV_RMSE=sqrt(mean((Predicted-Actual)^2)),
    CV_MAE=mean(abs(Predicted-Actual)),
    CV_R2=1-sum((Predicted-Actual)^2)/sum((Actual-mean(Actual))^2),.groups="drop") |>
  mutate(Complete=Predictions==nrow(amz_development)*amz_repeats) |>
  arrange(desc(Complete),CV_RMSE)
print(amz_cv_summary,n=Inf)
if(nrow(amz_cv_failures)) print(amz_cv_failures)
amz_eligible <- filter(amz_cv_summary,Complete)
if(!nrow(amz_eligible)) stop("No model completed every fold; inspect cv-failures.csv.")
amz_best_name <- amz_eligible$Model[1]
amz_best_spec <- amz_specs[match(amz_best_name,amz_specs$Model),,drop=FALSE]
cat("\nSelected by development CV RMSE:",amz_best_name,"\n")
write.csv(amz_cv_summary,file.path(amz_output_dir,"cv-model-comparison.csv"),row.names=FALSE)
write.csv(amz_cv_predictions,file.path(amz_output_dir,"cv-predictions.csv"),row.names=FALSE)
if(nrow(amz_cv_failures)) write.csv(amz_cv_failures,file.path(amz_output_dir,"cv-failures.csv"),row.names=FALSE)
amz_cv_plot <- ggplot(amz_cv_summary,aes(x=reorder(Model,CV_RMSE),y=CV_RMSE,fill=Complete))+
  geom_col()+coord_flip()+labs(title="Development cross-validation error",x=NULL,y="RMSE in dollars")+
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("TRUE"="#2878B5","FALSE"="#E76F51"))+theme_minimal(base_size=12)
amz_show_plot(amz_cv_plot)
ggsave(file.path(amz_output_dir,"cv-model-comparison.png"),amz_cv_plot,width=9,height=6,dpi=160)
```

## 6. Final fit and calibrated prediction intervals

The chosen model fits the development sample. Absolute errors on the separate
calibration sample determine a 90% split-conformal prediction interval for an
individual set's Amazon price. These intervals target marginal coverage for data
exchangeable with the observed-price sample. They do not promise 90% coverage in
every subgroup, for future release years, or for sets whose missing prices arise
from a different process. Keep this development fit for the calibrated intervals.
Refitting on calibration or test observations requires a new evaluation.

```{r amz-model-6}
if (!exists("amz_output_dir")) amz_output_dir <- "modeling-results"
dir.create(amz_output_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

# Freeze the model choice before looking at calibration or test errors.
amz_final_model <- amz_fit(amz_development,amz_best_spec,amz_seed+9000L)
amz_calibration_pred <- amz_predict(amz_final_model,amz_calibration)
amz_calibration_scores <- abs(amz_calibration$Amazon_Price-amz_calibration_pred)
amz_q_index <- min(length(amz_calibration_scores),
  ceiling((length(amz_calibration_scores)+1)*amz_interval_level))
amz_interval_radius <- sort(amz_calibration_scores)[amz_q_index]
amz_predict_interval <- function(model,newdata,radius=amz_interval_radius) {
  pred <- amz_predict(model,newdata)
  data.frame(Predicted=pred,Lower=pmax(0,pred-radius),Upper=pred+radius)
}
# This is a split-conformal interval for an individual Amazon price. It targets
# marginal coverage under exchangeability with the priced population, not
# coverage within every age/year/price subgroup. Shifted or unpriced sets may differ.
amz_test_pred <- amz_predict_interval(amz_final_model,amz_test)
amz_test_results <- cbind(amz_test[c("Item_Number","Set_Name","Year","Amazon_Price")],amz_test_pred)
amz_test_results$Error <- amz_test_results$Predicted-amz_test_results$Amazon_Price
amz_test_results$Covered <- with(amz_test_results,Amazon_Price>=Lower & Amazon_Price<=Upper)
amz_test_score <- amz_metrics(amz_test$Amazon_Price,amz_test_pred$Predicted)
amz_test_score$Model <- amz_best_name
amz_test_score$Interval_Level <- amz_interval_level
amz_test_score$Observed_Coverage <- mean(amz_test_results$Covered)
amz_test_score$Mean_Interval_Width <- mean(amz_test_pred$Upper-amz_test_pred$Lower)
print(amz_test_score)

# Predetermined reference models on the SAME final test sets. Do not use this
# comparison to change the selected model or tune another round of candidates.
amz_reference_scores <- bind_rows(lapply(c("Training mean","EDA linear"),function(name) {
  sp <- amz_specs[match(name,amz_specs$Model),,drop=FALSE]
  fit <- amz_fit(amz_development,sp,amz_seed+9001L)
  cbind(Model=name,amz_metrics(amz_test$Amazon_Price,amz_predict(fit,amz_test)))
}),cbind(Model=amz_best_name,amz_metrics(amz_test$Amazon_Price,amz_test_pred$Predicted))) |>
  distinct(Model,.keep_all=TRUE)
print(amz_reference_scores)
write.csv(amz_test_score,file.path(amz_output_dir,"selected-model-test-metrics.csv"),row.names=FALSE)
write.csv(amz_reference_scores,file.path(amz_output_dir,"test-reference-comparison.csv"),row.names=FALSE)
write.csv(amz_test_results,file.path(amz_output_dir,"test-predictions-and-intervals.csv"),row.names=FALSE)
```

## 7. Error patterns and model diagnostics

Positive Bias means overprediction, while negative Bias means underprediction.
The price-band table checks the presentation's concern about expensive sets, with
sample sizes shown for each band. The residual graph uses development predictions
from held-out CV folds instead of fitted training values. Large Cook's distances
flag observations for review in the EDA linear reference; they are not automatic
deletion rules. Forest importance ranks predictive contributions in this fit and
does not establish causation. Correlated features can share importance.

```{r amz-model-7}
if (!exists("amz_output_dir")) amz_output_dir <- "modeling-results"
dir.create(amz_output_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

amz_test_results$Price_Band <- factor(ifelse(amz_test_results$Amazon_Price<30,"Under $30",
  ifelse(amz_test_results$Amazon_Price<=100,"$30 to $100","Over $100")),
  levels=c("Under $30","$30 to $100","Over $100"))
amz_group_metrics <- function(dat,group) {
  bind_rows(lapply(split(dat,dat[[group]],drop=TRUE),function(x) {
    cbind(Group=as.character(x[[group]][1]),amz_metrics(x$Amazon_Price,x$Predicted),
      Coverage=mean(x$Covered),Mean_Actual=mean(x$Amazon_Price),Mean_Predicted=mean(x$Predicted))
  }))
}
amz_band_results <- amz_group_metrics(amz_test_results,"Price_Band")
amz_year_results <- amz_group_metrics(amz_test_results,"Year")
print(amz_band_results); print(amz_year_results)
write.csv(amz_band_results,file.path(amz_output_dir,"test-error-by-price-band.csv"),row.names=FALSE)
write.csv(amz_year_results,file.path(amz_output_dir,"test-error-by-release-year.csv"),row.names=FALSE)
amz_actual_plot <- ggplot(amz_test_results,aes(x=Amazon_Price,y=Predicted,color=Year))+
  geom_abline(slope=1,intercept=0,linetype="dashed",color="grey40")+
  geom_point(alpha=0.7)+coord_equal()+
  labs(title=paste("Final test predictions:",amz_best_name),x="Actual Amazon price ($)",y="Predicted price ($)")+
  theme_minimal(base_size=12)
amz_show_plot(amz_actual_plot)
ggsave(file.path(amz_output_dir,"test-actual-versus-predicted.png"),amz_actual_plot,width=8,height=6,dpi=160)
amz_oof <- amz_cv_predictions |> filter(Model==amz_best_name) |>
  group_by(Item_Number) |> summarise(Actual=first(Actual),Predicted=mean(Predicted),.groups="drop") |>
  mutate(Residual=Actual-Predicted)
amz_residual_plot <- ggplot(amz_oof,aes(x=Predicted,y=Residual))+
  geom_hline(yintercept=0,linetype="dashed")+geom_point(alpha=0.5,color="#2878B5")+
  geom_smooth(method="loess",formula=y~x,se=FALSE,color="#E76F51")+
  labs(title="Development errors from held-out folds",subtitle="Predictions averaged across CV repeats",
       x="Predicted Amazon price ($)",y="Actual minus predicted ($)")+theme_minimal(base_size=12)
amz_show_plot(amz_residual_plot)
ggsave(file.path(amz_output_dir,"development-residuals.png"),amz_residual_plot,width=8,height=6,dpi=160)
amz_largest_errors <- amz_test_results |> arrange(desc(abs(Error))) |> head(10)
print(amz_largest_errors)
# Influence diagnostics apply to the EDA linear reference. A large Cook's
# distance flags a set for review; it is not a rule for deleting expensive sets.
amz_eda_diagnostic_model <- amz_fit(amz_development,
  amz_specs[match("EDA linear",amz_specs$Model),,drop=FALSE],amz_seed+9100L)
amz_influence <- data.frame(amz_development[c("Item_Number","Set_Name","Amazon_Price")],
  Cooks_Distance=cooks.distance(amz_eda_diagnostic_model$fit),
  Leverage=hatvalues(amz_eda_diagnostic_model$fit),
  Studentized_Residual=rstudent(amz_eda_diagnostic_model$fit)) |>
  arrange(desc(Cooks_Distance))
print(head(amz_influence,10))
write.csv(amz_influence,file.path(amz_output_dir,"eda-linear-influence.csv"),row.names=FALSE)
if(amz_best_spec$Engine=="forest") {
  imp <- randomForest::importance(amz_final_model$fit,type=1)
  amz_importance <- data.frame(Feature=rownames(imp),Permutation_Importance=as.numeric(imp[,1])) |>
    arrange(desc(Permutation_Importance))
  print(head(amz_importance,15))
  write.csv(amz_importance,file.path(amz_output_dir,"selected-model-variable-importance.csv"),row.names=FALSE)
} else if(amz_best_spec$Engine %in% c("lm","gamma")) {
  print(summary(amz_final_model$fit))
  # Coefficients/p-values after CV selection are descriptive, not confirmatory.
}
```

## 8. LEGO recommended price as a generalizability check

The assignment's generalizability question is whether a model trained on
Amazon price also predicts LEGO recommended price. We answer that by comparing
the frozen Amazon-model predictions with both targets on the same paired test
sets. The additional listed-price benchmark instead asks how well LEGO's price
alone approximates Amazon's price. That benchmark never enters model fitting or
selection. Different target variances affect R-squared, and differences in dollar
error or bias should also guide the interpretation. Amazon-calibrated intervals
have no coverage guarantee for LEGO prices.

```{r amz-model-8}
if (!exists("amz_output_dir")) amz_output_dir <- "modeling-results"
dir.create(amz_output_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

# The selected AMAZON model and its predictions are now frozen. Evaluate its
# point predictions against LEGO prices for held-out sets with both targets.
# This is response transfer, distinct from using LEGO Price to predict Amazon.
amz_lego_price <- amz_number(amz_raw$Price)
amz_lego_lookup <- setNames(amz_lego_price,as.character(amz_raw$Item_Number))
amz_transfer <- amz_test_results
amz_transfer$LEGO_Price <- unname(amz_lego_lookup[amz_transfer$Item_Number])
amz_transfer <- amz_transfer[is.finite(amz_transfer$LEGO_Price) & amz_transfer$LEGO_Price>0,]
amz_transfer_scores <- bind_rows(
  cbind(Target="Amazon price on paired test sets",amz_metrics(amz_transfer$Amazon_Price,amz_transfer$Predicted)),
  cbind(Target="LEGO price on paired test sets",amz_metrics(amz_transfer$LEGO_Price,amz_transfer$Predicted)))
print(amz_transfer_scores)
# An additional descriptive purchasing benchmark on exactly those same sets.
amz_lego_benchmark <- amz_metrics(amz_transfer$Amazon_Price,amz_transfer$LEGO_Price)
print(cbind(Benchmark="Use LEGO listed price as Amazon estimate",amz_lego_benchmark))
write.csv(amz_transfer_scores,file.path(amz_output_dir,"lego-price-generalizability.csv"),row.names=FALSE)
write.csv(amz_transfer,file.path(amz_output_dir,"paired-test-price-check.csv"),row.names=FALSE)
```

## 9. Predictions for unpriced sets and a reusable saved model

The final export estimates Amazon prices for the 478 unpriced sets. Their true
Amazon prices remain unknown, so these rows cannot measure accuracy. Review the
missing-value, unseen-category, and extrapolation flags before using an estimate
for a purchasing decision. A prediction truncated to zero is a model boundary
failure that needs manual review, rather than evidence that a set is free. The
saved model stores preprocessing, calibration, split membership, and package
versions. The example at the end shows how to apply it to another raw-data file.

```{r amz-model-9}
if (!exists("amz_output_dir")) amz_output_dir <- "modeling-results"
dir.create(amz_output_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

amz_support_flags <- function(dat,prep) {
  vapply(seq_len(nrow(dat)),function(i) {
    reasons <- character()
    for(v in amz_num) {
      if(is.na(dat[[v]][i])) reasons <- c(reasons,paste("Missing",v))
      else if(dat[[v]][i]<prep$ranges[[v]][1] || dat[[v]][i]>prep$ranges[[v]][2]) {
        reasons <- c(reasons,paste(v,"outside development range"))
      }
    }
    for(v in amz_cat) {
      val <- dat[[v]][i]; if(is.na(val)) val <- "Missing"
      if(!val %in% prep$categories[[v]]$seen) reasons <- c(reasons,paste("Unseen",v))
    }
    if(length(reasons)) paste(reasons,collapse="; ") else "Within observed predictor support"
  },character(1))
}
amz_missing_predictions <- cbind(amz_unpriced[c("Item_Number","Set_Name","Year")],
  amz_predict_interval(amz_final_model,amz_unpriced))
amz_missing_predictions$Review_Flags <- amz_support_flags(amz_unpriced,amz_final_model$prep)
amz_zero_predictions <- amz_missing_predictions$Predicted<=0
amz_missing_predictions$Review_Flags[amz_zero_predictions] <- paste(
  amz_missing_predictions$Review_Flags[amz_zero_predictions],
  "Nonpositive model estimate truncated to $0; manual review",sep="; ")
amz_missing_predictions$Status <- "Estimated Amazon price; actual Amazon price unavailable"
print(head(amz_missing_predictions,10))
write.csv(amz_missing_predictions,file.path(amz_output_dir,"unpriced-set-predictions.csv"),row.names=FALSE)
amz_model_bundle <- list(model=amz_final_model,interval_radius=amz_interval_radius,
  interval_level=amz_interval_level,split=amz_membership,seed=amz_seed,
  cv_results=amz_cv_summary,test_metrics=amz_test_score,
  package_versions=vapply(amz_packages,function(p) as.character(packageVersion(p)),character(1)))
saveRDS(amz_model_bundle,file.path(amz_output_dir,"amazon-price-model.rds"))
writeLines(capture.output(sessionInfo()),file.path(amz_output_dir,"session-info.txt"))
# Example for a FUTURE raw-data file with the same predictor columns:
# bundle <- readRDS("modeling-results/amazon-price-model.rds")
# new_raw <- readr::read_csv("new-lego-sets.csv",locale=readr::locale(encoding="Latin1"))
# new_raw$Amazon_Price <- NA_character_ # no response needed at prediction time
# new_sets <- amz_clean(new_raw)
# amz_predict_interval(bundle$model,new_sets,bundle$interval_radius)
# amz_support_flags(new_sets,bundle$model$prep)
# Keep the development fit for these calibrated intervals. Refitting on the
# calibration/test rows invalidates both the reported test evaluation and this
# calibration radius. A later refit needs new calibration and validation data.
```

## Interpretation and reporting

- Report the selected model, the CV selection rule, the split sizes, test RMSE,
  MAE, R-squared, bias, and observed prediction interval coverage.
- Compare all candidate models using CV, rather than repeatedly choosing based
  on the final test set. The presentation and this analysis use different splits
  and training procedures, so their test RMSE values are not directly comparable.
- Check whether year and age add information beyond the original EDA predictors.
  The dedicated comparison and the expanded regression help assess that question.
- Discuss missingness and the fact that validation describes sets with observed
  Amazon prices. Performance for unpriced sets or future releases remains uncertain.
- Coefficient tests after model selection are exploratory. The goal here is
  prediction, with all substantive effects interpreted conditionally and cautiously.
